stem: A patient opens his eyes to pain, makes incomprehensible sounds and withdraws from a painful stimulus. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale score?
explanation: Eye opening to pain scores 2 (E2), incomprehensible sounds 2 (V2) and withdrawal 4 (M4), giving a total of 8. Abnormal flexion scores 3 and extension 2. A GCS of 8 or less generally indicates severe brain injury and need for airway protection.
referenceText: Carney et al. 2017 (Brain Trauma Foundation, 4th ed.) [31]; ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]

stem: According to the Brain Trauma Foundation 4th edition, at what ICP threshold should treatment be initiated, and what is the recommended CPP target range?

options.B: ICP above 40 mmHg; CPP below 50 mmHg
options.D: ICP above 15 mmHg; CPP above 100 mmHg
options.E: ICP above 10 mmHg; CPP 90–100 mmHg

explanation: BTF 4th edition recommends treating ICP above 22 mmHg, associated with increased mortality, and a CPP target of 60–70 mmHg. Aggressive attempts to maintain CPP above 70 mmHg with fluids and pressors are avoided because of ARDS risk.
referenceText: Carney et al. 2017 (Brain Trauma Foundation, 4th ed.) [31]

stem: What is the BTF recommendation regarding hyperventilation in severe TBI?

options.A: Hyperventilation is the first-line treatment for raised ICP
options.B: Prophylactic hyperventilation to PaCO2 ≤25 mmHg is not recommended; brief use only for herniation
options.C: Hypercapnia should be induced to improve cerebral blood flow
options.D: Routine hyperventilation to PaCO2 25 mmHg for 72 hours
options.E: Hyperventilation should be used only during the first 24 hours, when cerebral blood flow is high

explanation: Hypocapnia causes cerebral vasoconstriction, reducing ICP but also cerebral blood flow, risking ischaemia, especially in the first 24 hours when flow is often critically reduced. BTF recommends against prolonged prophylactic hyperventilation; normocapnia (35–45 mmHg) is targeted.
referenceText: Carney et al. 2017 (Brain Trauma Foundation, 4th ed.) [31]

stem: A patient with severe TBI has ICP 30 mmHg despite sedation and head elevation. Serum sodium is 138 mmol/L and osmolality 300 mOsm/kg. Which is an appropriate next step?

options.C: Fluid restriction and furosemide only, avoiding all osmotic agents
options.E: Hyperosmolar therapy: mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg or hypertonic saline

explanation: Mannitol and hypertonic saline lower ICP by creating an osmotic gradient and improving rheology. Mannitol causes osmotic diuresis and hypovolaemia; repeat doses are often withheld if the osmolar gap is high (above about 20) or osmolality exceeds 320 mOsm/kg. Hypertonic saline is preferred in hypovolaemia.
referenceText: Carney et al. 2017 (Brain Trauma Foundation, 4th ed.) [31]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: What is the recommendation regarding corticosteroids in moderate or severe traumatic brain injury?

options.A: Corticosteroids are recommended only with ICP above 30 mmHg
options.B: Corticosteroids are not recommended because they increase mortality
options.C: Hydrocortisone should be given to all patients
options.D: High-dose methylprednisolone within 8 hours improves outcome
options.E: Dexamethasone reduces ICP from cerebral oedema in TBI

explanation: The CRASH trial showed increased mortality with high-dose methylprednisolone in TBI. BTF gives a Level I recommendation against steroids for improving outcome or reducing ICP. Dexamethasone is useful for vasogenic oedema around tumours, not traumatic oedema.
referenceText: Carney et al. 2017 (Brain Trauma Foundation, 4th ed.) [31]

stem: What did the DECRA trial show regarding early bifrontotemporoparietal decompressive craniectomy for diffuse TBI with moderately raised ICP?

options.A: It reduced the incidence of hydrocephalus
options.B: It increased mortality but improved function
options.C: It lowered ICP and ICU stay but worsened 6-month functional outcome
options.D: It improved 6-month functional outcome and reduced mortality in all patients
options.E: It had no effect on ICP

explanation: DECRA enrolled patients with diffuse TBI and ICP above 20 mmHg for 15 minutes despite first-tier therapy. Early craniectomy reduced ICP and ICU days but worsened extended Glasgow Outcome Scale scores. BTF does not recommend bifrontal decompression for early moderate ICP elevations.
referenceText: Cooper et al. 2011 (DECRA) [40]; Carney et al. 2017 (Brain Trauma Foundation, 4th ed.) [31]

stem: In the RESCUEicp trial, secondary decompressive craniectomy for refractory ICP above 25 mmHg resulted in which outcome compared with medical management?

options.A: Higher mortality and worse functional outcome at 12 months in the surgical arm
options.E: Lower mortality but more vegetative state or severe disability

explanation: RESCUEicp randomised patients with refractory intracranial hypertension (above 25 mmHg) to craniectomy or continued medical care including barbiturates. Mortality at 6 months was lower (26.9% vs 48.9%) but rates of vegetative state and lower or upper severe disability were higher, raising questions about acceptable outcomes.
referenceText: Hutchinson et al. 2016 (RESCUEicp) [98]; Carney et al. 2017 (Brain Trauma Foundation, 4th ed.) [31]

stem: What is the BTF recommendation regarding seizure prophylaxis after severe TBI?

options.B: Long-term phenytoin for 1 year to prevent late post-traumatic epilepsy
options.C: Phenytoin (or levetiracetam) to reduce early seizures within 7 days
options.E: No prophylaxis; treat only clinical seizures

explanation: BTF recommends phenytoin to decrease early post-traumatic seizures (within 7 days) when benefits outweigh risks; it does not prevent late seizures. Levetiracetam is widely used, with insufficient evidence to recommend it over phenytoin.
referenceText: Carney et al. 2017 (Brain Trauma Foundation, 4th ed.) [31]

stem: In the CRASH-3 trial, which patients with TBI appeared to benefit from tranexamic acid given within 3 hours of injury?

options.C: Patients with bilateral unreactive pupils on arrival
options.E: Patients treated after 8 hours

explanation: CRASH-3 randomised over 12,000 TBI patients. TXA within 3 hours reduced head-injury-related death in mild-to-moderate TBI, without increased vascular occlusive events, but not in severe TBI with unreactive pupils. Earlier treatment was more effective.
referenceText: CRASH-3 Collaborators 2019 [42]

stem: According to BTF, what systolic BP should be maintained in a 30-year-old patient with severe TBI?

options.E: At least 160 mmHg

explanation: BTF recommends maintaining systolic BP of at least 100 mmHg for patients aged 50–69 years and at least 110 mmHg for those aged 15–49 or over 70 years. A single episode of hypotension is associated with doubled mortality in TBI.
referenceText: Carney et al. 2017 (Brain Trauma Foundation, 4th ed.) [31]

stem: A patient with expanding intracranial haematoma develops hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration. What does this triad indicate?

options.B: Severely raised ICP with impending brainstem herniation
options.E: Autonomic dysreflexia from spinal cord injury

explanation: The Cushing triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing) is a late sign of raised ICP and brainstem compression. It requires immediate measures to lower ICP (osmotherapy, brief hyperventilation) and urgent neurosurgical intervention.
referenceText: Carney et al. 2017 (Brain Trauma Foundation, 4th ed.) [31]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: A patient with an acute left subdural haematoma develops a dilated, unreactive left pupil and right-sided hemiparesis. What is the mechanism?

options.D: Subfalcine herniation compressing the anterior cerebral artery and corpus callosum
options.E: Left uncal herniation compressing the left oculomotor nerve and cerebral peduncle

explanation: Uncal herniation compresses the ipsilateral third nerve (dilated pupil) and cerebral peduncle (contralateral hemiparesis). Occasionally the contralateral peduncle is compressed against the tentorium (Kernohan notch), causing ipsilateral hemiparesis, a false localising sign.
referenceText: Carney et al. 2017 (Brain Trauma Foundation, 4th ed.) [31]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: What threshold of brain tissue oxygen tension (PbtO2) is generally considered to indicate brain hypoxia requiring intervention?

options.E: Below 20 mmHg

explanation: PbtO2 values below about 20 mmHg are associated with worse outcomes, and below 10 mmHg indicate severe hypoxia. Management includes optimising CPP, oxygenation, haemoglobin and PaCO2. BOOST-3 is evaluating whether PbtO2-guided therapy improves outcome.
referenceText: Carney et al. 2017 (Brain Trauma Foundation, 4th ed.) [31]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: A patient with TBI has MAP 80 mmHg and ICP 25 mmHg. What is the cerebral perfusion pressure?

options.E: 105 mmHg

explanation: CPP = MAP − ICP = 80 − 25 = 55 mmHg, below the BTF target of 60–70 mmHg. Management includes lowering ICP and/or raising MAP. The arterial transducer should be zeroed at the level of the tragus (foramen of Monro) for accurate CPP.
referenceText: Carney et al. 2017 (Brain Trauma Foundation, 4th ed.) [31]

stem: What is the recommended nimodipine regimen in aneurysmal SAH?

options.A: Nimodipine only if vasospasm is seen on angiography
options.D: 240 mg orally once daily for 3 months
options.E: 60 mg orally or enterally every 4 hours for 21 days

explanation: Oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days improves neurological outcome after aneurysmal SAH, probably through neuroprotection rather than reversing angiographic vasospasm. If hypotension occurs, dosing can be changed to 30 mg every 2 hours.
referenceText: Hoh et al. 2023 (AHA/ASA aneurysmal SAH) [92]

stem: A patient with aneurysmal SAH has an unsecured aneurysm and BP 190/100 mmHg. What is appropriate early management?

options.A: Give prophylactic hypervolaemic therapy before securing
options.B: Allow BP up to 220/120 mmHg until aneurysm repair at day 10
options.C: Delay aneurysm securing for 2 weeks, to allow cerebral oedema and vasospasm risk to settle completely
options.D: Control severe hypertension (e.g. SBP <160 mmHg) and secure the aneurysm early, ideally within 24 h
options.E: Start therapeutic heparin to prevent vasospasm

explanation: Rebleeding is greatest in the first 24 hours. Early aneurysm securing (endovascular coiling or clipping) is recommended, and extreme hypertension is avoided before securing. Short-course antifibrinolytics before repair are not shown to improve outcome.
referenceText: Hoh et al. 2023 (AHA/ASA aneurysmal SAH) [92]

stem: Seven days after aneurysmal SAH with a coiled aneurysm, a patient develops new right arm weakness and drowsiness. CT shows no new haemorrhage or hydrocephalus. Which approach is recommended?

options.A: Maintain euvolaemia; consider induced hypertension and endovascular rescue therapy
options.D: Prophylactic hypervolaemic haemodilution (triple-H therapy) for 7 days in all patients
options.E: Stop nimodipine

explanation: Delayed cerebral ischaemia peaks at days 4–14. Euvolaemia should be maintained; prophylactic hypervolaemia and haemodilution are not recommended. Induced hypertension (in a secured aneurysm) and intra-arterial vasodilators or angioplasty are used for symptomatic vasospasm, although evidence is limited.
referenceText: Hoh et al. 2023 (AHA/ASA aneurysmal SAH) [92]

stem: A patient with SAH becomes drowsy on day 1; CT shows enlarged temporal horns and ventricles. What is the most appropriate management?

options.E: Lumbar puncture to remove 50 mL of CSF before aneurysm securing

explanation: Acute hydrocephalus occurs in 20–30% after SAH and causes reduced consciousness. External ventricular drainage is recommended; it may improve neurological grade. Permanent shunting is reserved for chronic shunt-dependent hydrocephalus.
referenceText: Hoh et al. 2023 (AHA/ASA aneurysmal SAH) [92]

stem: A patient with SAH has GCS 13 without focal deficit. What is the World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies (WFNS) grade?

options.E: Grade V

explanation: WFNS grades: I = GCS 15; II = GCS 13–14 without motor deficit; III = GCS 13–14 with motor deficit; IV = GCS 7–12; V = GCS 3–6. Higher grades predict poorer outcome. The modified Fisher scale grades CT blood load and predicts vasospasm.
referenceText: Hoh et al. 2023 (AHA/ASA aneurysmal SAH) [92]

stem: A patient with high-grade SAH develops pulmonary oedema, troponin rise and regional wall motion abnormalities that do not match a coronary distribution. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.D: Neurogenic stunned myocardium from catecholamine surge
options.E: Infective endocarditis

explanation: Neurogenic stunned myocardium results from sympathetic surge and catecholamine-mediated myocardial injury, often with Takotsubo-like patterns. It is usually reversible. Inotropes (dobutamine, milrinone) may be needed to maintain cerebral perfusion; thrombolysis is contraindicated.
referenceText: Hoh et al. 2023 (AHA/ASA aneurysmal SAH) [92]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: A patient with spontaneous ICH of 15 mL has systolic BP 195 mmHg 2 hours after onset. What does the 2022 AHA/ASA guideline suggest?

options.B: Lowering systolic BP to below 110 mmHg
options.C: No treatment unless BP exceeds 230 mmHg
options.D: Maintain systolic BP above 180 mmHg to preserve perfusion of the perihaematomal tissue
options.E: Lower systolic BP to about 140 mmHg (range 130–150), avoiding falls below 130

explanation: In mild-to-moderate ICH with systolic BP 150–220 mmHg, acute lowering to a target of 140 mmHg (130–150) is safe and may improve functional outcome; lowering below 130 mmHg may be harmful. Smooth, sustained control with minimal variability is recommended.
referenceText: Greenberg et al. 2022 (AHA/ASA intracerebral haemorrhage) [82]

stem: A patient on warfarin with INR 3.2 presents with ICH. What is the recommended reversal?

options.C: Four-factor PCC plus IV vitamin K
options.E: Vitamin K orally alone

explanation: 4F-PCC corrects INR faster than FFP with less volume and is recommended in warfarin-associated ICH, together with IV vitamin K 5–10 mg to sustain reversal. FFP is used only when PCC is unavailable; rFVIIa is not recommended.
referenceText: Greenberg et al. 2022 (AHA/ASA intracerebral haemorrhage) [82]; Tomaselli et al. 2020 (ACC oral anticoagulant bleeding pathway) [214]

stem: A patient taking dabigatran presents with ICH. What is the specific reversal agent?

options.E: Vitamin K

explanation: Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran and reverses its effect within minutes. Andexanet alfa or PCC are used for factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban). Haemodialysis can remove dabigatran if idarucizumab is unavailable.
referenceText: Greenberg et al. 2022 (AHA/ASA intracerebral haemorrhage) [82]; Tomaselli et al. 2020 (ACC oral anticoagulant bleeding pathway) [214]

stem: What did the PATCH trial show about platelet transfusion for ICH in patients on antiplatelet therapy who did not require surgery?

options.A: Platelet transfusion reduced haematoma expansion and mortality
options.E: Platelet transfusion was associated with worse functional outcome

explanation: PATCH showed that platelet transfusion increased death or dependence at 3 months in antiplatelet-associated ICH not needing surgery. AHA/ASA guidance recommends against platelet transfusion in this setting; it may be considered before emergency neurosurgery.
referenceText: Baharoglu et al. 2016 (PATCH) [13]; Greenberg et al. 2022 (AHA/ASA intracerebral haemorrhage) [82]

stem: A patient has a 4-cm cerebellar haemorrhage with brainstem compression, obstructive hydrocephalus and declining consciousness. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Urgent surgical evacuation of the haematoma
options.C: External ventricular drain alone, without surgery
options.E: Hyperventilation for 72 hours

explanation: In cerebellar ICH with neurological deterioration, brainstem compression and/or hydrocephalus, immediate surgical evacuation is recommended; EVD alone is not recommended because of upward herniation risk. Supratentorial ICH surgery has less clear benefit.
referenceText: Greenberg et al. 2022 (AHA/ASA intracerebral haemorrhage) [82]

stem: A patient presents 2 hours after onset of acute ischaemic stroke and is eligible for IV thrombolysis. BP is 200/115 mmHg. What is required?

options.A: Lower BP below 185/110 before thrombolysis, then ≤180/105 mmHg for 24 hours
options.B: Lower BP to 120/80 mmHg before thrombolysis
options.D: Delay thrombolysis until BP normalises spontaneously
options.E: Thrombolysis is contraindicated at this BP, whatever antihypertensive is given

explanation: AHA/ASA recommend lowering BP to below 185/110 mmHg (e.g. with labetalol, nicardipine or clevidipine) before IV thrombolysis and maintaining it at or below 180/105 mmHg for 24 hours afterwards to reduce symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage.
referenceText: Powers et al. 2019 (AHA/ASA acute ischaemic stroke) [168]

stem: A patient with a proximal MCA occlusion is seen 14 hours after last known well. Perfusion imaging shows a small infarct core with large mismatch. What does the 2019 AHA/ASA guideline recommend?

options.D: Mechanical thrombectomy; DAWN/DEFUSE 3-eligible patients benefit up to 24 hours
options.E: IV thrombolysis at 14 hours as the only reperfusion option, without imaging selection

explanation: DAWN and DEFUSE 3 showed benefit from thrombectomy between 6 and 24 hours (DAWN) or 6 and 16 hours (DEFUSE 3) in patients with large vessel occlusion and favourable imaging (mismatch). The 2019 guideline recommends thrombectomy in such patients.
referenceText: Powers et al. 2019 (AHA/ASA acute ischaemic stroke) [168]

stem: A 52-year-old with a large right MCA infarction deteriorates on day 2 with midline shift on CT. What is the most effective intervention?

options.E: Mannitol alone for 7 days

explanation: In patients aged 60 or younger with malignant MCA infarction deteriorating within 48 hours, decompressive hemicraniectomy reduces mortality and improves functional outcome. Benefits in older patients are smaller and survival with disability is more common. Steroids are not recommended for cerebral oedema in stroke.
referenceText: Powers et al. 2019 (AHA/ASA acute ischaemic stroke) [168]

stem: A patient has a generalised convulsion lasting 7 minutes. IV access is available. What is the recommended first-line treatment?

options.B: IV lorazepam 4 mg (0.1 mg/kg), repeated once if needed
options.D: IV phenytoin 20 mg/kg before any benzodiazepine
options.E: Oral diazepam

explanation: Convulsive status epilepticus is defined operationally as seizure lasting 5 minutes or more. Benzodiazepines are first-line: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (up to 4 mg per dose), IM midazolam 10 mg if no IV access, or IV diazepam. Under-dosing is common and reduces success.
referenceText: Glauser et al. 2016 (AES convulsive status epilepticus) [77]; Brophy et al. 2012 (NCS status epilepticus) [26]

stem: In the ESETT trial of benzodiazepine-refractory status epilepticus, how did levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate compare?

options.B: All three had similar efficacy, stopping seizures in about half
options.C: Valproate was inferior, with more hypotension and arrhythmia than the other two drugs
options.E: None of the agents had any effect

explanation: ESETT randomised patients with benzodiazepine-refractory status epilepticus to levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg or valproate 40 mg/kg; seizure cessation and improved responsiveness occurred in about 45–47% with each, with similar adverse events.
referenceText: Kapur et al. 2019 (ESETT) [110]

stem: Seizures continue despite lorazepam and levetiracetam. The patient is intubated. What is the next step?

options.A: Wait 24 hours for levetiracetam to take full effect before escalating any treatment
options.C: Continuous anaesthetic infusion (e.g. midazolam or propofol) with continuous EEG
options.E: A third benzodiazepine bolus and observe

explanation: Refractory status epilepticus (persisting after a benzodiazepine and one second-line agent) requires continuous anaesthetic infusions (midazolam, propofol, ketamine or pentobarbital) with EEG to target seizure suppression or burst suppression. Paralysis without EEG masks ongoing seizures.
referenceText: Brophy et al. 2012 (NCS status epilepticus) [26]

stem: A patient remains comatose 1 hour after convulsions have stopped following treatment of status epilepticus. What investigation is recommended?

options.D: Continuous EEG to exclude non-convulsive status epilepticus
options.E: No investigation; drowsiness is expected for 48 hours

explanation: NCS guidance recommends continuous EEG within 1 hour if the patient does not return to baseline within 10 minutes after seizure cessation or remains comatose for 60 minutes, because non-convulsive seizures occur in up to half of such patients and require treatment.
referenceText: Brophy et al. 2012 (NCS status epilepticus) [26]

stem: What is the maximum recommended IV infusion rate of phenytoin and the main reason for this limit?

options.A: 100 mg/min, to avoid hyperglycaemia and peripheral vein irritation
options.C: 50 mg/min in adults, to limit hypotension and arrhythmias
options.E: No limit applies

explanation: Phenytoin infusion rates above 50 mg/min (lower in the elderly and those with heart disease) cause hypotension, bradycardia and arrhythmias, partly from the propylene glycol vehicle. Fosphenytoin can be infused faster (up to 150 mg PE/min). Extravasation causes purple glove syndrome.
referenceText: Brophy et al. 2012 (NCS status epilepticus) [26]; Nelson et al. 2019 (Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies) [151]

stem: A patient with status epilepticus controlled on IV valproate is started on meropenem for pneumonia and develops recurrent seizures. What is the most likely explanation?

options.C: Carbapenems markedly reduce serum valproate concentrations
options.E: Meropenem directly lowers the seizure threshold more than any other drug

explanation: Carbapenems inhibit acylpeptide hydrolase, reducing valproate concentrations by up to 90% within 24 hours; increasing the valproate dose does not overcome this. An alternative antiepileptic or antibiotic should be used.
referenceText: Brophy et al. 2012 (NCS status epilepticus) [26]; Nelson et al. 2019 (Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies) [151]

stem: A patient with Guillain–Barré syndrome is unable to walk unaided 5 days after onset. What is the recommended disease-modifying treatment?

options.A: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days, then an oral prednisolone taper
options.E: IV immunoglobulin 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days, or plasma exchange

explanation: IVIG and plasma exchange are equally effective when started within 2 weeks (IVIG) or 4 weeks (plasma exchange) in patients who cannot walk unaided. Corticosteroids are ineffective. Combining both treatments sequentially offers no added benefit.
referenceText: Shahrizaila et al. 2021 (Guillain–Barré syndrome) [195]

stem: Which finding indicates the need for elective intubation in a patient with Guillain–Barré syndrome?

options.A: Oxygen saturation of 94% on room air
options.C: Mild dysphagia with a normal vital capacity and an effective cough
options.D: VC <20 mL/kg, MIP weaker than −30 cmH2O or MEP <40 cmH2O
options.E: Respiratory rate of 18/min

explanation: The "20/30/40 rule" identifies impending respiratory failure in neuromuscular disease. Hypoxaemia and hypercapnia are late signs. Rapid progression, bulbar dysfunction, bilateral facial weakness and autonomic instability also predict need for ventilation.
referenceText: Shahrizaila et al. 2021 (Guillain–Barré syndrome) [195]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: A patient with myasthenia gravis develops worsening weakness and respiratory failure after treatment for pneumonia. Which antibiotic class is most likely to have precipitated the crisis?

options.E: Aminoglycosides or fluoroquinolones

explanation: Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, magnesium, beta-blockers and neuromuscular blockers can worsen neuromuscular transmission and precipitate myasthenic crisis. Infection itself is the most common trigger.
referenceText: Sanders et al. 2016 (myasthenia gravis consensus) [188]

stem: A patient in myasthenic crisis is intubated for respiratory failure. What is the recommended rapid-acting immunotherapy?

options.A: High-dose prednisolone alone started on day 1 without other therapy
options.B: Increase pyridostigmine to high doses while ventilated
options.E: Thymectomy within 24 hours

explanation: Plasma exchange and IVIG produce rapid improvement in myasthenic crisis; plasma exchange may act faster. Corticosteroids are added but can cause initial worsening. Pyridostigmine is often withheld in ventilated patients to reduce secretions and avoid cholinergic crisis.
referenceText: Sanders et al. 2016 (myasthenia gravis consensus) [188]

stem: Which condition must be met for the apnoea test in determining death by neurological criteria?

options.A: PaCO2 ≥60 mmHg and ≥20 mmHg above baseline, with no respiratory effort
options.C: Respiratory effort is assessed while the patient remains on pressure support ventilation
options.D: Systolic BP of 70 mmHg is acceptable
options.E: The test is performed with a body temperature of 33 °C

explanation: The World Brain Death Project requires prerequisites (established cause, exclusion of confounders, normothermia ≥36 °C, SBP ≥100 or MAP ≥60 mmHg, absence of drug effects) and an apnoea test demonstrating no breathing with PaCO2 ≥60 mmHg and ≥20 mmHg above baseline, while the patient is oxygenated off pressure support.
referenceText: Greer et al. 2020 (World Brain Death Project) [83]

stem: When are ancillary tests required for determining death by neurological criteria?

options.A: Only when the family requests them
options.B: When the apnoea test is positive
options.D: When examination cannot be completed or confounders cannot be excluded
options.E: In every patient, as a mandatory component of the diagnosis in all jurisdictions

explanation: Ancillary tests (e.g. four-vessel angiography, CT angiography, radionuclide perfusion, transcranial Doppler) assess cerebral blood flow and are used when parts of the examination or apnoea test cannot be performed or confounders persist. EEG alone is not recommended as an ancillary test in adults by the World Brain Death Project.
referenceText: Greer et al. 2020 (World Brain Death Project) [83]

stem: A 62-year-old presents with fever, neck stiffness and confusion. Which empirical regimen is recommended in an area with pneumococcal cephalosporin resistance?

options.A: Ceftriaxone alone, started only after CT head and lumbar puncture have both been completed
options.C: Dexamethasone with or before antibiotics, plus ceftriaxone, vancomycin and amoxicillin
options.E: Amoxicillin alone

explanation: ESCMID recommends dexamethasone 10 mg every 6 hours for 4 days, started with or just before antibiotics, which reduces mortality in pneumococcal meningitis. Empirical therapy is a third-generation cephalosporin, plus vancomycin or rifampicin where resistance is prevalent, plus amoxicillin for Listeria in patients over 50 or immunocompromised.
referenceText: van de Beek et al. 2016 (ESCMID bacterial meningitis) [222]

stem: Which patient with suspected bacterial meningitis should have cranial imaging before lumbar puncture?

options.A: A young patient with fever and neck stiffness but normal consciousness
options.B: Every patient regardless of clinical features
options.C: A patient with a petechial rash
options.D: A patient with focal neurological deficits, new-onset seizures or GCS below 10
options.E: A patient with photophobia only

explanation: ESCMID recommends imaging before LP in patients with focal neurological deficits (excluding cranial nerve palsies), new-onset seizures, severely altered consciousness (GCS below 10) or severe immunocompromise. Antibiotics and dexamethasone should never be delayed for imaging.
referenceText: van de Beek et al. 2016 (ESCMID bacterial meningitis) [222]

stem: A patient presents with fever, confusion, behavioural change and seizures. MRI shows left temporal lobe signal abnormality. What treatment should be started immediately?

options.E: Corticosteroids alone

explanation: HSV encephalitis is the most common sporadic fatal encephalitis; temporal lobe involvement is typical. IV aciclovir (10 mg/kg every 8 hours, adjusted for renal function, for 14–21 days) must be started empirically without waiting for CSF PCR, as delay worsens outcome.
referenceText: Tunkel et al. 2008 (IDSA encephalitis) [217]

stem: A patient with acute traumatic cervical spinal cord injury is admitted to ICU. Which management is supported by the AANS/CNS guidelines?

options.C: Allow MAP to fall to 55 mmHg to reduce bleeding into the injured spinal cord
options.D: Maintain MAP about 85–90 mmHg for 7 days and avoid methylprednisolone
options.E: Delayed intubation until respiratory arrest

explanation: AANS/CNS 2013 guidelines suggest maintaining MAP at 85–90 mmHg for the first 7 days to optimise spinal cord perfusion, and recommend against methylprednisolone because of harms without proven benefit. High cervical injuries often need early airway management.
referenceText: Walters et al. 2013 (AANS/CNS acute spinal cord injury) [231]

stem: A kidney transplant recipient on tacrolimus develops headache, visual disturbance, seizures and severe hypertension. MRI shows bilateral parieto-occipital vasogenic oedema. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.E: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy

explanation: PRES is associated with hypertension, eclampsia, renal failure and immunosuppressants (calcineurin inhibitors) or chemotherapy. It produces vasogenic oedema mainly in posterior regions. Treatment is BP control, seizure management and withdrawal of the precipitating drug; it is usually reversible.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; ACOG 2020 (Practice Bulletin 222) [4]

stem: A postpartum woman has headache, seizures and a haemorrhagic venous infarct; MR venography shows superior sagittal sinus thrombosis. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Immediate systemic thrombolysis in all patients with sinus thrombosis
options.B: Anticoagulation with heparin despite the haemorrhagic infarct
options.E: Aspirin only

explanation: AHA/ASA guidance recommends anticoagulation with UFH or LMWH for CVT, even with haemorrhagic venous infarction, because haemorrhage results from venous congestion. Endovascular therapy is considered for deterioration despite anticoagulation; decompressive surgery for impending herniation.
referenceText: Saposnik et al. 2011 (AHA/ASA cerebral venous thrombosis) [189]

stem: Which patient is an appropriate candidate for ICP monitoring according to BTF?

options.A: A patient with GCS 14 and normal CT
options.B: A salvageable patient with severe TBI (GCS 3–8) and an abnormal CT
options.C: A patient with a cervical spine fracture but no clinical or radiological head injury
options.E: A patient with GCS 15 and a small skull fracture

explanation: BTF 3rd edition criteria (still widely used) recommend ICP monitoring for salvageable patients with severe TBI (GCS 3–8) and an abnormal CT, or with normal CT if two or more of age over 40, motor posturing or systolic BP below 90 mmHg are present. The 4th edition notes management guided by ICP reduces in-hospital and 2-week mortality.
referenceText: Carney et al. 2017 (Brain Trauma Foundation, 4th ed.) [31]

stem: Ten days after severe diffuse axonal injury, a patient has episodes of tachycardia, hypertension, tachypnoea, fever, diaphoresis and posturing triggered by turning and suctioning. Infection has been excluded. What is the most likely diagnosis and treatment?

options.A: Status epilepticus; treat with phenytoin only
options.B: Paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity; treat with opioids, propranolol, gabapentin or clonidine
options.D: Septic shock; treat with broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.E: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome from antipsychotics; treat with dantrolene and bromocriptine

explanation: Paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity follows severe acquired brain injury and causes episodic sympathetic surges. Diagnosis requires exclusion of sepsis, seizures and withdrawal. Treatment includes minimising triggers, opioids, propranolol, gabapentin, clonidine and benzodiazepines.
referenceText: Carney et al. 2017 (Brain Trauma Foundation, 4th ed.) [31]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: What did the Eurotherm3235 trial show for therapeutic hypothermia (32–35 °C) to treat raised ICP after TBI?

options.A: Hypothermia eliminated the need for osmotherapy and improved survival at 6 months
options.B: Hypothermia plus standard care gave worse functional outcome than standard care
options.E: Hypothermia plus standard care resulted in worse functional outcome than standard care alone

explanation: Eurotherm3235 found that hypothermia lowered ICP but resulted in worse functional outcomes and was stopped early. BTF recommends against early, short-term prophylactic hypothermia in diffuse injury; normothermia should be maintained.
referenceText: Andrews et al. 2015 (Eurotherm3235) [7]; Carney et al. 2017 (Brain Trauma Foundation, 4th ed.) [31]

stem: A malnourished patient with alcohol use disorder is confused, ataxic and has nystagmus. Before IV dextrose, what should be given?

options.D: High-dose IV thiamine (e.g. 200–500 mg three times daily)
options.E: Oral folic acid and vitamin B12 supplements, then dextrose

explanation: Wernicke encephalopathy results from thiamine deficiency and presents with confusion, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus and ataxia (the full triad is often absent). High-dose parenteral thiamine is required, and glucose before thiamine can precipitate or worsen it. Untreated, it progresses to Korsakoff syndrome.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Nelson et al. 2019 (Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies) [151]
